description: Anatomical and morphological observations of the female breast. Dimensions are drawn from established plastic-surgery, dermatology, oncology, and aesthetic-anthropometry literature. The schema is comprehensive — some dimensions are not assessable from a single photograph and are flagged accordingly via the `observability` block.

dimensions.scale_citation: Halls MH (1998). Aesthetic Plastic Surgery, 22(5). Extended with categories described in subsequent plastic-surgery literature (Mallucci & Branford 2014; Goldwyn 1999).
dimensions.description: Overall morphology of the breast envelope, classified along an extended categorical scheme combining the original Halls (1998) shape classes with widely-used additions from subsequent aesthetic-anatomy literature.

values.definition: Symmetric upper- and lower-pole fullness with approximately equal projection above and below the nipple-areolar complex (NAC). Base width approximates projection.
Less upper-pole fullness than lower; greater projection below the NAC than above. NAC sits at or near the apex of projection.
Wider base, smaller volume, more muscular and less subcutaneous-fat envelope. Projection is reduced relative to base width.
Narrow base with conical projection; reduced volume; pointed apex at or near the NAC.

Volume or shape difference greater than approximately one-half cup size between left and right breasts. Used when asymmetry is the dominant morphological feature, not as a fine-grained quantification.
Constricted base diameter, herniated parenchyma into the areola, narrow inframammary fold, and elevated NAC. Per Grolleau et al. (1999) classification.
Lateral splay of the NAC away from midline; intermammary distance approximates or exceeds breast base diameter. Common variant noted in aesthetic-anatomy literature.

dimensions.scale_citation: Regnault P (1976). Breast ptosis: definition and treatment. Clinics in Plastic Surgery, 3(2): 193-203.
dimensions.description: Degree of breast ptosis (descent) defined by the position of the nipple relative to the inframammary fold (IMF) and the lower breast pole.

values.definition: Nipple sits above the IMF; breast tissue is firm and contained above the IMF.
Nipple at the level of the IMF, above the lower breast contour.
Nipple below the IMF but above the lower breast contour. NAC visible from frontal view as the most projected point of the lower pole.
Nipple below the IMF and at or below the lower breast contour, pointing downward.
Nipple above the IMF, but the breast tissue itself has descended below the IMF — glandular ptosis without NAC ptosis.

observability.notes: Best assessed from lateral or three-quarter view; frontal view alone can underestimate grade III.

dimensions.scale_citation: Visual proxy for US bra cup-size convention. Volumetric measurement (per Bouman 1994; Smith et al. 1986) is the academically-rigorous alternative but requires direct measurement, not a photograph.
dimensions.description: Visual estimate of breast size mapped onto the US cup-size convention, treated as an ordinal scale. Subject to image-angle, posture, and clothing variance; should not be treated as a measured dimension.

observability.notes: Clothing, posture, and camera angle introduce substantial variance. Treat as soft signal, not measurement.

dimensions.scale_citation: Mallucci P, Branford OA (2014). Concepts in aesthetic breast dimensions. Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, 134(1): 8e-16e.
dimensions.description: Width of the breast base as a fraction of chest-wall width. Relative measure rather than absolute distance.

values.definition: Base diameter substantially less than half of chest-wall width.
Base diameter approximately one-third to one-half of chest-wall width.
Base diameter approaching or exceeding half of chest-wall width.

dimensions.scale_citation: Mallucci P, Branford OA (2014). Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, 134(1).
dimensions.description: Anterior projection of the breast relative to base diameter. Distinguishes flatter from more conical morphologies independent of overall size.

values.definition: Projection less than ~40% of base diameter.
Projection ~40-60% of base diameter.
Projection greater than ~60% of base diameter.

dimensions.scale_citation: Mallucci P, Branford OA (2014). Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, 134(1): 8e-16e. Defines the aesthetic 45:55 upper-pole-to-lower-pole proportion as the reference for natural breast shape.
dimensions.description: Convexity of the upper pole between the clavicle and the NAC. The Mallucci-Branford paper identifies the upper-pole slope as a primary determinant of perceived natural shape.

values.definition: Upper pole slopes inward from clavicle to NAC; insufficient soft-tissue fill.
Upper pole forms a straight line from approximately the second intercostal space to the NAC. Considered the aesthetic reference per Mallucci & Branford 2014.
Upper pole bulges outward; over-projection above the natural reference line.

observability.notes: Best assessed from lateral or three-quarter view.

dimensions.scale_citation: Mallucci P, Branford OA (2014). Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, 134(1).
dimensions.description: Distribution of breast volume in the lower pole — between the NAC and the inframammary fold (IMF). Paired with `upper_pole_fullness`; together these capture the 45:55 aesthetic ratio when both are 'balanced'.

values.definition: Lower pole carries less than ~50% of breast volume; gland feels superior-shifted.
Lower pole carries approximately 55% of volume; aesthetic reference per Mallucci & Branford.
Lower pole substantially overfilled relative to upper; common with ptosis and post-lactational changes.

dimensions.scale_citation: Boutros S, Kattash M, Wienfeld A, et al. (1998). The intradermal anatomy of the inframammary fold. Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, 102(4).
dimensions.description: Sharpness of the IMF as a visible anatomical landmark.

values.definition: Clearly defined fold with a crisp transition from breast to chest wall.
Gradual transition; fold visible but not crisp.
Fold not clearly visible; breast tissue blends gradually into the chest wall — common in tuberous and constricted-base morphologies.

dimensions.scale_citation: Hauben DJ, Mahler D (1983). A reappraisal of the importance of areolar pigmentation. Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, 71(6). Normative areolar-diameter ranges discussed; relative-to-base scale used here as a photo-friendly proxy.
dimensions.description: Diameter of the areola relative to the breast base diameter, treated as ordinal.

values.definition: Areolar diameter less than ~25% of breast base diameter.
Areolar diameter approximately 25-40% of breast base diameter.
Areolar diameter greater than ~40% of breast base diameter.

dimensions.scale_citation: Pigmentation gradient described qualitatively; Fitzpatrick I–VI does not directly map to areolar pigmentation, which can be substantially darker than surrounding breast skin (Hauben & Mahler 1983).
dimensions.description: Pigmentation intensity of the areolar complex, observed independently of overall skin Fitzpatrick category.

values.definition: Pink or near-skin-tone; minimal pigmentation contrast against breast skin.
Slightly pigmented; visible contrast against breast skin.
Moderately pigmented; tan or light brown.
Strongly pigmented; medium to dark brown.
Deep brown to nearly black pigmentation.

observability.notes: Lighting and color balance affect this dimension significantly; the model should defer to lower confidence under poor lighting.

dimensions.scale_citation: Hoffman classification of nipple inversion, as commonly cited in breastfeeding-medicine and aesthetic-surgery literature (e.g., Han & Hong 1999, extending Hoffman's original framework).
dimensions.description: Morphology of the nipple itself, including inversion grading.

values.definition: Nipple protrudes outward at rest. The typical configuration.
Nipple level with the areola at rest; protrudes with cold or stimulation.
Nipple inverted at rest but easily everts manually or with stimulation; no fibrotic banding.
Nipple inverted; everts with difficulty and retracts when released; mild fibrotic banding.
Nipple permanently inverted; cannot be manually everted; significant fibrotic banding.

observability.notes: Distinguishing flat from grade-I inversion typically requires manual assessment; photographs allow only static evaluation.

dimensions.scale_citation: Brody GS (1981). Aesthetic and reconstructive symmetry assessment. Surveyed in subsequent aesthetic-surgery literature.
dimensions.description: Degree of symmetry between left and right breasts.

values.definition: No discernible asymmetry.
Small but observable difference in volume, shape, or NAC position; less than approximately one-quarter cup difference.
Difference of approximately one-half cup or comparable shape difference.
Difference of one full cup or greater, or substantial shape divergence.

dimensions.scale_citation: American College of Radiology (2013). BI-RADS Atlas, 5th Edition.
dimensions.description: Mammographic breast density classification. Included in the schema for completeness; assessment requires X-ray imaging and is not derivable from a photograph.

observability.notes: Density is a mammographic finding; the analysis prompt should not attempt to infer this from a photograph. Included in the schema so structured-text use cases can populate it from clinical data when available.

dimensions.scale_citation: Marshall WA, Tanner JM (1969). Variations in pattern of pubertal changes in girls. Archives of Disease in Childhood, 44(235): 291-303.
dimensions.description: Tanner stage of breast development (B1 to B5). Used in pediatric-endocrinology and developmental-anthropology literature.

values.definition: No glandular tissue; flat appearance.
Small mound of breast tissue with areolar enlargement.
Further breast and areolar enlargement; no separation of contours.
Areola and papilla project above the breast as a secondary mound.
Areola recesses to the general breast contour; mature adult morphology.

observability.notes: Almost all dataset rows from notable-people photographs will be B5. Lower stages should not appear in adult-only sources; if observed, the source-attribution chain needs review.

references: Regnault P (1976). Clinics in Plastic Surgery, 3(2): 193-203.
Mallucci P, Branford OA (2014). Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, 134(1): 8e-16e.
Hauben DJ, Mahler D (1983). Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, 71(6).
Boutros S, Kattash M, Wienfeld A, et al. (1998). Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, 102(4).
Grolleau JL, et al. (1999). Tuberous-breast classification. Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, 104(7).
Marshall WA, Tanner JM (1969). Archives of Disease in Childhood, 44(235): 291-303.
American College of Radiology (2013). BI-RADS Atlas, 5th Edition.
Bouman FG (1994). Volumetric measurement of the human breast. Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, 93(5).
Smith DJ, et al. (1986). Breast volume by photogrammetry. Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, 78(2).
